claim: Fluoride ion channels of the Fluc family combat toxicity arising from accumulation of environmental F-.
source: Fluoride ion channels of the Fluc family combat toxicity arising from accumulation of environmental F-.
evidence: This is a statement about the biological function of Fluc channels, drawing on established scientific understanding of these channels.

claim: A ladder of H-bond donating residues creates a 'polar track' demarking the ion-conduction pathway.
source: A ladder of H-bond donating residues creates a 'polar track' demarking the ion-conduction pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and mutagenesis experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Track polarity is functionally dispensable at several positions.
source: Surprisingly, while track polarity is well conserved, polarity is nonetheless functionally dispensable at several positions.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis data showing that alanine substitutions at certain polar track positions retain activity.

claim: A threonine at one end of the pore engages in vital interactions through its β-branched methyl group.
source: A threonine at one end of the pore engages in vital interactions through its β-branched methyl group.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis data showing that Val and Ile substitutions at T114 retain activity while Ser does not.

claim: Two critical central phenylalanines directly coordinate F- through a quadrupolar-ion interaction.
source: Two critical central phenylalanines that directly coordinate F- through a quadrupolar-ion interaction cannot be functionally substituted by aromatic, non-polar, or polar sidechains.
evidence: This is supported by crystal structures showing F- coordination by phenylalanine residues and by established knowledge of quadrupolar interactions.

claim: The two critical central phenylalanines cannot be functionally substituted by aromatic, non-polar, or polar sidechains.
source: Two critical central phenylalanines that directly coordinate F- through a quadrupolar-ion interaction cannot be functionally substituted by aromatic, non-polar, or polar sidechains.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis data showing that Y, W, H, S, T, Q, L, and A substitutions at F80 and F83 abolish activity.

claim: Methionine is the only functional replacement for phenylalanine at position 80.
source: The only functional replacement is methionine, which coordinates F- through its partially positive γ-methylene in mimicry of phenylalanine's quadrupolar interaction.
evidence: This is supported by flux assays and single-channel recordings showing F80M retains near-WT activity.

claim: Methionine coordinates F- through its partially positive γ-methylene in mimicry of phenylalanine's quadrupolar interaction.
source: The only functional replacement is methionine, which coordinates F- through its partially positive γ-methylene in mimicry of phenylalanine's quadrupolar interaction.
evidence: This is supported by crystal structures of F80M showing the γ-methylene positioned near F- and by electrostatic reasoning.

claim: Aqueous fluoride ion inhibits certain phosphoryl-transfer enzymes critical for energy production and nucleic acid synthesis.
source: Aqueous fluoride ion is an omnipresent environmental xenobiotic that inhibits certain phosphoryl-transfer enzymes critical for energy production and nucleic acid synthesis (Marquis et al., 2003; Samygina et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Two phylogenetically unrelated F- efflux systems resist the toxicity of cellular F-: the CLCF family of F-/H+ antiporters, and the Fluc family of F- ion channels.
source: Two phylogenetically unrelated F- efflux systems are now known that resist the toxicity of cellular F-: the CLCF family of F-/H+ antiporters, and the Fluc family of F- ion channels (Baker et al., 2012; Stockbridge et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Fluc channels are present in all classes of life except higher animals.
source: Fluc channels, present in all classes of life except higher animals, allow passive transit of F- ions across the membrane down their electrochemical gradient.
evidence: This is a statement about the phylogenetic distribution of Fluc channels, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: Fluc channels allow passive transit of F- ions across the membrane down their electrochemical gradient.
source: Fluc channels, present in all classes of life except higher animals, allow passive transit of F- ions across the membrane down their electrochemical gradient.
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism of Fluc channels, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: Bacterial Fluc channels are constructed as small, dual-topology dimers.
source: Bacterial Fluc channels are constructed as small, dual-topology dimers; the two subunits, each of ~120 residues, span the membrane in opposite orientations to form the functional complex (Stockbridge et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The two subunits of bacterial Fluc channels, each of ~120 residues, span the membrane in opposite orientations to form the functional complex.
source: Bacterial Fluc channels are constructed as small, dual-topology dimers; the two subunits, each of ~120 residues, span the membrane in opposite orientations to form the functional complex (Stockbridge et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Fluc channels exhibit exceptionally high F-/Cl- selectivity.
source: These channels are notable for this unusual architecture as well as for exceptionally high F-/Cl-selectivity.
evidence: This is supported by functional data cited in the manuscript.

claim: Crystal structures of two Fluc channels reveal four bound F- ions.
source: Recent crystal structures of two Fluc channels (Stockbridge et al., 2015; Last et al., 2016) reveal four bound F- ions whose transmembrane disposition imply two antiparallel ion-permeation pathways, each occupied simultaneously by two F- ions (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: The transmembrane disposition of four bound F- ions implies two antiparallel ion-permeation pathways, each occupied simultaneously by two F- ions.
source: Recent crystal structures of two Fluc channels (Stockbridge et al., 2015; Last et al., 2016) reveal four bound F- ions whose transmembrane disposition imply two antiparallel ion-permeation pathways, each occupied simultaneously by two F- ions (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference from structural data presented in cited literature and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Each ion-permeation pathway in Fluc channels was postulated to be extremely narrow, largely anhydrous, and filled up by side chains that hand off F- ions passing along it.
source: Each pathway was postulated to be extremely narrow, largely anhydrous, and filled up by side chains that hand off F- ions passing along it (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural observations shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Substitutions of three conserved, ion-coordinating residues (two phenylalanines and an asparagine) fully inhibit F- transport.
source: This unusual structural inference was confirmed functionally by substitutions of three conserved, ion-coordinating residues in this region – two phenylalanines and an asparagine – that fully inhibit F- transport.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis data from prior studies.

claim: Two bound F- ions in a single pore are separated by 12 Å.
source: Zooming in on a single pore of the Fluc homologue under study here (Figure 1b), we see two bound F- ions separated by 12 Å and surrounded mainly by protein side chains.
evidence: This is a measurement from the crystal structure shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The lower F- ion in the pore approaches one of the wide aqueous vestibules on the two ends of the channel.
source: The lower ion approaches one of the wide aqueous vestibules on the two ends of the channel, while the other is deeply buried within the protein.
evidence: This is an observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 1b.

claim: One F- ion in the pore is deeply buried within the protein.
source: The lower ion approaches one of the wide aqueous vestibules on the two ends of the channel, while the other is deeply buried within the protein.
evidence: This is an observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Two conserved Phe residues each coordinate a F- ion in an electropositive edge-on orientation.
source: The proposed critical pore-associated moieties are of two chemical types: aromatic rings of two conserved Phe residues contributed from different subunits, each of which coordinates a F- ion in an electropositive edge-on orientation, and dipolar H-bond donors arranged to satisfy the F- ion's H-bond accepting preference.
evidence: This is supported by crystal structures and electrostatic reasoning.

claim: Dipolar H-bond donors are arranged to satisfy the F- ion's H-bond accepting preference.
source: The proposed critical pore-associated moieties are of two chemical types: aromatic rings of two conserved Phe residues contributed from different subunits, each of which coordinates a F- ion in an electropositive edge-on orientation, and dipolar H-bond donors arranged to satisfy the F- ion's H-bond accepting preference.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural observations and chemical reasoning.

claim: H-bonding residues form a 'polar track' extending in both directions beyond the centrally located Phe rings.
source: These H-bonding residues were proposed (Stockbridge et al., 2015) to form a 'polar track' extending in both directions beyond the centrally located Phe rings, as indicated in the sequence alignment and structure of Figure 1.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior work, supported by structural data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Most polar track residues emanate from TM4, where they appear at every 4th position.
source: Most polar track residues emanate from TM4, where they appear at every 4th position, and although not all are individually conserved, H-bond donors frequently appear here.
evidence: This is an observation from sequence alignments and structural data.

claim: Although not all polar track residues are individually conserved, H-bond donors frequently appear at these positions.
source: Most polar track residues emanate from TM4, where they appear at every 4th position, and although not all are individually conserved, H-bond donors frequently appear here.
evidence: This is an observation from sequence alignments.

claim: Several polar track residues coordinate F- ions in the crystal structures.
source: Several of these coordinate F- ions in the crystal structures, while others lie close to the aqueous vestibules where crystallographically ordered waters are also observed.
evidence: This is an observation from crystal structures.

claim: Some polar track residues lie close to the aqueous vestibules where crystallographically ordered waters are observed.
source: Several of these coordinate F- ions in the crystal structures, while others lie close to the aqueous vestibules where crystallographically ordered waters are also observed.
evidence: This is an observation from crystal structures.

claim: The Fluc pore structures do not show water-filled aqueous tunnels lined by polar groups.
source: We emphasize that the structures do not show water-filled aqueous tunnels lined by polar groups, as in many other ion channels; instead, the pores are filled with a web of side chains (Figure 1c) that must be negotiated by ions translocating at rates on the order of 106–107 ions/sec.
evidence: This is an observation from crystal structures shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The Fluc pores are filled with a web of side chains that must be negotiated by ions translocating at rates on the order of 10^6–10^7 ions/sec.
source: We emphasize that the structures do not show water-filled aqueous tunnels lined by polar groups, as in many other ion channels; instead, the pores are filled with a web of side chains (Figure 1c) that must be negotiated by ions translocating at rates on the order of 106–107 ions/sec.
evidence: This combines structural observations with functional measurements of ion flux rates.

claim: A Fluc homologue from an E. coli virulence plasmid, nicknamed 'Ec2', was used for all experiments.
source: A Fluc homologue from an E. coli virulence plasmid, nicknamed 'Ec2' (Stockbridge et al., 2013), was used for all experiments.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental system used in the study.

claim: Three strongly conserved, deeply buried residues (F80, F83, N41) spanning ~7 Å along the pore are required for transport.
source: Three strongly conserved, deeply buried residues spanning ~7 Å along the pore were previously found to be required for transport (Stockbridge et al., 2015; Last et al., 2016) in this and a different homologue: two Phe (F80, F83) and an Asn positioned between them (N41).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior mutagenesis studies.

claim: S84A, S102A, and S110A mutants display single-channel conductances within 25% of WT.
source: Surprisingly, we find (Figure 2b) that F- robustly permeates three track mutants denuded of their hydroxyl groups - S84A, S102A, and S110A - with single-channel conductances within 25% of WT (Figure 2c, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by single-channel recording data shown in Figure 2c and Table 1.

claim: H106A, T114A, H106S, H106Y, H106W, H106N, H106F, N41S, N41Q, and N41Y mutants are completely nonfunctional.
source: In contrast, H106A and T114A, as well as alternative H-bonding substitutes H106S, H106Y, H106W, H106N, H106F, N41S, N41Q, and N41Y are completely nonfunctional (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), representing >10,000 fold rate-inhibition relative to WT.
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nonfunctional mutants H106A, T114A, and related substitutions represent >10,000 fold rate-inhibition relative to WT.
source: In contrast, H106A and T114A, as well as alternative H-bonding substitutes H106S, H106Y, H106W, H106N, H106F, N41S, N41Q, and N41Y are completely nonfunctional (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), representing >10,000 fold rate-inhibition relative to WT.
evidence: This is an inference from the flux assay's detection limit and time response.

claim: H106 coordinates a partially hydrated F- ion located close to bulk solvent at one end of the narrow pore.
source: In crystal structures (Figure 1b) H106 coordinates a partially hydrated F- ion located close to bulk solvent at one end of the narrow pore, T114 lies beyond the other F- ion at the opposite end, and the other residues tested reside between them.
evidence: This is an observation from crystal structures shown in Figure 1b.

claim: T114 lies beyond the F- ion at the opposite end of the pore from H106.
source: In crystal structures (Figure 1b) H106 coordinates a partially hydrated F- ion located close to bulk solvent at one end of the narrow pore, T114 lies beyond the other F- ion at the opposite end, and the other residues tested reside between them.
evidence: This is an observation from crystal structures shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Functionally sensitive positions chart out a ~20 Å span connecting the deepest parts of the aqueous vestibules.
source: These functionally sensitive positions thus chart out a ~ 20 Å span connecting the deepest parts of the aqueous vestibules, as suggested from the structures alone.
evidence: This is an inference combining mutagenesis data with structural measurements.

claim: Aromatic substitutions (Y, W, H) at the central Phe positions completely abolish channel activity.
source: Aromatics (Y, W, H) were introduced as conservative substitutions, aliphatic H-bond donors (S, T, Q) as potential F--coordination partners of alternative chemistry, and hydrophobic aliphatics (L, A) as additional controls. All eight mutations, most of them tested at both Phe residues, completely abolish channel activity (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Aliphatic H-bond donor substitutions (S, T, Q) at the central Phe positions completely abolish channel activity.
source: Aromatics (Y, W, H) were introduced as conservative substitutions, aliphatic H-bond donors (S, T, Q) as potential F--coordination partners of alternative chemistry, and hydrophobic aliphatics (L, A) as additional controls. All eight mutations, most of them tested at both Phe residues, completely abolish channel activity (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hydrophobic aliphatic substitutions (L, A) at the central Phe positions completely abolish channel activity.
source: Aromatics (Y, W, H) were introduced as conservative substitutions, aliphatic H-bond donors (S, T, Q) as potential F--coordination partners of alternative chemistry, and hydrophobic aliphatics (L, A) as additional controls. All eight mutations, most of them tested at both Phe residues, completely abolish channel activity (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The F80Y crystal structure is essentially identical to WT with Cα rmsd ~0.3 Å.
source: A crystal structure of the F80Y mutant, solved to assess F- binding and structure of the pore region, is essentially identical to WT (Cα rmsd ~0.3 Å) with the Tyr ring congruent to that of WT Phe (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a measurement from crystallographic data shown in Figure 3b and supplements.

claim: In the F80Y structure, the Tyr ring is congruent to that of WT Phe.
source: A crystal structure of the F80Y mutant, solved to assess F- binding and structure of the pore region, is essentially identical to WT (Cα rmsd ~0.3 Å) with the Tyr ring congruent to that of WT Phe (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 3b.

claim: F- remains bound to the F80Y mutant in precisely the same positions as in WT.
source: In contrast to previous structures of inactive Ile mutants (Last et al., 2016), F- remains bound to the Tyr construct in precisely the same positions as in WT (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Previous structures of inactive Ile mutants showed loss of F- binding.
source: In contrast to previous structures of inactive Ile mutants (Last et al., 2016), F- remains bound to the Tyr construct in precisely the same positions as in WT (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a reference to prior structural data.

claim: No significant structural changes between WT and the inactive F80Y mutant are apparent.
source: Other than the added hydroxyl group, no significant structural changes between WT and the inactive F80Y mutant are apparent, nor does the structure suggest a clear reason why F- fails to permeate the mutant.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing crystal structures.

claim: The F80Y structure does not suggest a clear reason why F- fails to permeate the mutant.
source: Other than the added hydroxyl group, no significant structural changes between WT and the inactive F80Y mutant are apparent, nor does the structure suggest a clear reason why F- fails to permeate the mutant.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of obvious structural differences.

claim: Some bacterial Fluc sequences are homodimeric while others are known or inferred heterodimers.
source: Bacterial Fluc sequences present a complication that must be appreciated in interpreting alignments. While many Fluc proteins are homodimeric like Ec2, others are known or inferred heterodimers as in Lactobacillus acidophilus (La1, La2), Staphylococcus aureus (Sa1, Sa2), and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mt1, Mt2).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and prior knowledge.

claim: In heterodimeric Fluc channels, one of the two pores may become inactivated through genetic drift.
source: This circumstance offers the possibility of genetic drift, such that one of the two pores becomes inactivated. As long as the second pore remains active, the inactivated pore can lose residues vital for transport with no physiological effect.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on evolutionary reasoning.

claim: Both La and Sa heterodimers retain three of the central phenylalanines, but have either Leu or Met at the fourth position.
source: Thus, both La and Sa heterodimers retain three of the central phenylalanines, but have either Leu or Met appear at the fourth position.
evidence: This is an observation from sequence alignments.

claim: The Mt heterodimer loses both phenylalanines at the second position, replaced with either methionine or tryptophan.
source: The Mt heterodimer surprisingly loses both phenylalanines at the second position, replaced with either methionine or tryptophan.
evidence: This is an observation from sequence alignments.

claim: Met or Trp may be capable of coordinating and transporting fluoride in the Mt heterodimer.
source: This leads to the unexpected hypothesis that that either Met or Trp are capable of coordinating and transporting fluoride in that construct.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on sequence observations.

claim: The electron-withdrawing sulfur in Met produces a partial positive charge on the γ-methylene and terminal methyl groups.
source: In this context, Met can be viewed as a uniquely plausible non-aromatic substitute for Phe, since the electron-withdrawing sulfur is expected to produce a partial positive charge on the γ-methylene and terminal methyl groups, either of which might act as an electrostatic surrogate to coordinate F-.
evidence: This is based on established chemical knowledge about sulfur's electronegativity.

claim: The γ-methylene or terminal methyl groups of Met might act as an electrostatic surrogate to coordinate F-.
source: In this context, Met can be viewed as a uniquely plausible non-aromatic substitute for Phe, since the electron-withdrawing sulfur is expected to produce a partial positive charge on the γ-methylene and terminal methyl groups, either of which might act as an electrostatic surrogate to coordinate F-.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on electrostatic reasoning.

claim: F80M results in an active flux-phenotype.
source: Remarkably, F80M results in an active flux-phenotype (Figure 3c) and displays clean single-channel recordings with near-WT conductance (Figure 3d, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: F80M displays clean single-channel recordings with near-WT conductance.
source: Remarkably, F80M results in an active flux-phenotype (Figure 3c) and displays clean single-channel recordings with near-WT conductance (Figure 3d, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by single-channel recording data shown in Figure 3d and Table 1.

claim: F83M is inactive.
source: In contrast, F83M is inactive.
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data.

claim: The F80M and F83M crystal structures are virtually identical to WT with Cα rmsd ~0.3 Å from WT.
source: We determined crystal structures of both Met mutants to test the prediction above regarding F- coordination. As with the Tyr substitute, the Met structures are virtually identical to WT (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), and all residues surrounding the substitutions are unmoved (Cα rmsd ~0.3 Å from WT, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a measurement from crystallographic data shown in Figure 3b and supplements.

claim: All residues surrounding the Met substitutions are unmoved in the crystal structures.
source: We determined crystal structures of both Met mutants to test the prediction above regarding F- coordination. As with the Tyr substitute, the Met structures are virtually identical to WT (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), and all residues surrounding the substitutions are unmoved (Cα rmsd ~0.3 Å from WT, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from crystal structures shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The Met side chains in both F80M and F83M take on a twisted conformation, filling approximately the same space as the Phe ring in WT.
source: The Met side chains in both take on a twisted conformation, filling approximately the same space as the Phe ring in WT.
evidence: This is an observation from crystal structures.

claim: In both Met mutants, F- ions are coordinated by the γ-methylenes located in nearly the same positions as the coordinating Phe ring carbons in WT.
source: As predicted, in both Met mutants F- ions are coordinated by the γ-methylenes located in nearly the same positions as the coordinating Phe ring carbons in WT (Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4), as though the substituted linear side chains attempt to mimic Phe's aromatic ring in occupied volume and F--binding electrostatics.
evidence: This is an observation from crystal structures shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: The substituted Met side chains attempt to mimic Phe's aromatic ring in occupied volume and F--binding electrostatics.
source: As predicted, in both Met mutants F- ions are coordinated by the γ-methylenes located in nearly the same positions as the coordinating Phe ring carbons in WT (Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4), as though the substituted linear side chains attempt to mimic Phe's aromatic ring in occupied volume and F--binding electrostatics.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural similarity of F- coordination.

claim: The similar structures of F80Y, F80M, and F83M offer no explanation why F80M is functionally active and F83M is not.
source: As with the Tyr mutant, the similar structures offer no explanation why F80M is functionally active and F83M is not.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of obvious structural differences.

claim: T114 lies at one end of the polar track, distant from bound F- ions.
source: As described above, the moderately conserved Thr114 lies at one end of the polar track, distant from bound F- ions, and its substitution by Ala abolishes channel activity, as if its hydroxyl group is necessary for ushering the anion into the narrow pore from the aqueous vestibule.
evidence: This is an observation from crystal structures and mutagenesis data.

claim: T114A substitution abolishes channel activity.
source: As described above, the moderately conserved Thr114 lies at one end of the polar track, distant from bound F- ions, and its substitution by Ala abolishes channel activity, as if its hydroxyl group is necessary for ushering the anion into the narrow pore from the aqueous vestibule.
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data.

claim: T114S is completely inactive.
source: However, a stark refutation of this idea emerges from the complete inactivity of T114S (Figure 4a), despite a T114S crystal structure showing the Ser hydroxyl exactly overlaying its WT counterpart and no significant structural changes elsewhere (Cα rmsd ~0.2 Å, Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The T114S crystal structure shows the Ser hydroxyl exactly overlaying its WT counterpart.
source: However, a stark refutation of this idea emerges from the complete inactivity of T114S (Figure 4a), despite a T114S crystal structure showing the Ser hydroxyl exactly overlaying its WT counterpart and no significant structural changes elsewhere (Cα rmsd ~0.2 Å, Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The T114S crystal structure shows no significant structural changes elsewhere with Cα rmsd ~0.2 Å.
source: However, a stark refutation of this idea emerges from the complete inactivity of T114S (Figure 4a), despite a T114S crystal structure showing the Ser hydroxyl exactly overlaying its WT counterpart and no significant structural changes elsewhere (Cα rmsd ~0.2 Å, Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a measurement from crystallographic data shown in Figure 4b and supplements.

claim: Val and Ile are fully active substitutes at position 114.
source: This perplexing result motivated an examination of Thr's β-branched methyl group as a functional determinant, and indeed Val and Ile were found to be fully active substitutes here in both liposome F- efflux and single-channel recording experiments (Figure 4a,c, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by flux assay and single-channel recording data shown in Figure 4a,c and Table 1.

claim: The T114 methyl group contacts the Gly49 Cα, V85 Cα, and F88 side chain from the partner subunit.
source: What could be the function of the β-branched methyl group? In the WT structure, this contacts the Gly49 Cα, V85 Cα, and F88 side chain, all from the partner subunit (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The T114 methyl may participate in a nonpolar interaction critical for stabilizing the conducting structure of WT.
source: Thus, it is possible that the T114 methyl participates in a nonpolar interaction critical for stabilizing the conducting structure of WT (a structure that nevertheless is still observed in T114S crystals).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural observations.

claim: F88A shows a smaller flux kinetic height than WT, demonstrating that a significant fraction of channels are inactive.
source: The height of the F88A flux kinetic is clearly smaller than that of WT (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), demonstrating that a significant fraction of the channels, although apparently well-folded and dimeric off the gel-filtration column, are inactive.
evidence: This is an observation from flux assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Active F88A channels have near WT levels of single channel flux.
source: However, those channels that remain active have near WT levels of single channel flux (Figure 4—figure supplement 4, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by single-channel recording data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4 and Table 1.

claim: Fluc channels exhibit extreme (>10,000 fold) selectivity against Cl- ions.
source: A striking feature of Fluc channels is their extreme (>10,000 fold) selectivity against Cl- ions (Stockbridge et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior functional data.

claim: No Cl- leakage is observed through any of the functional mutants described.
source: Whatever the mechanism of Cl- exclusion, though, it is preserved in all functional mutants described here; in no case do we observe any Cl- leakage through these channels (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), a result further supporting the structural propriety of the mutant channels independent of their crystal structures.
evidence: This is supported by Cl- efflux assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The absence of Cl- leakage in functional mutants supports the structural propriety of the mutant channels.
source: Whatever the mechanism of Cl- exclusion, though, it is preserved in all functional mutants described here; in no case do we observe any Cl- leakage through these channels (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), a result further supporting the structural propriety of the mutant channels independent of their crystal structures.
evidence: This is an inference from the functional data.

claim: The F- permeation pathway of Fluc channels remains mysterious despite functional experiments and crystal structures.
source: Despite functional experiments accompanied by crystal structures at resolution high enough to locate F- ions, revealing two parallel and independent pores, the F- permeation pathway of Fluc channels remains mysterious.
evidence: This is a summary statement reflecting the current state of understanding.

claim: The plug of sidechains clogging the pore leaves no clearly visible ion-diffusion pathway.
source: The plug of sidechains clogging the pore leaves no clearly visible ion-diffusion pathway, thus provoking our proposal for an unconventional 'channsporter' permeation mechanism (Stockbridge et al., 2015) whereby F- passage is accomplished by concomitant movements of side-chain rotamers on a submicrosecond timescale.
evidence: This is an observation from crystal structures.

claim: A 'channsporter' permeation mechanism has been proposed whereby F- passage is accomplished by concomitant movements of side-chain rotamers on a submicrosecond timescale.
source: The plug of sidechains clogging the pore leaves no clearly visible ion-diffusion pathway, thus provoking our proposal for an unconventional 'channsporter' permeation mechanism (Stockbridge et al., 2015) whereby F- passage is accomplished by concomitant movements of side-chain rotamers on a submicrosecond timescale.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed in prior work and cited here.

claim: The overall trajectory of the pore, from the solvent-accessible binding site at F83/H106 to the terminus near T114, is as suggested from the structures.
source: Experiments here have now delineated the critical residues along the length of the pore (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1); its overall trajectory, from the solvent-accessible binding site at F83/H106 to the terminus near T114, is as suggested from the structures, but several of the new findings are unexpected.
evidence: This is a conclusion combining structural and functional data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The failure of Tyr to functionally substitute for Phe at either Ec2 position is surprising in light of the F80Y crystal structure.
source: The failure of even Tyr to functionally substitute for Phe at either Ec2 position is particularly surprising in light of the F80Y crystal structure.
evidence: This is an inference from the combination of functional and structural data.

claim: In the F80Y structure, the Tyr and Phe rings and the F- ions adopt identical positions.
source: The Tyr and Phe rings and the F- ions adopt identical positions, and the Tyr hydroxyl points away from the bound F-, its presence leaving other parts of the protein undisturbed.
evidence: This is an observation from the F80Y crystal structure.

claim: The Tyr hydroxyl in F80Y points away from the bound F-.
source: The Tyr and Phe rings and the F- ions adopt identical positions, and the Tyr hydroxyl points away from the bound F-, its presence leaving other parts of the protein undisturbed.
evidence: This is an observation from the F80Y crystal structure.

claim: Modification of ring electrostatics by the polarizable hydroxyl may lead to a more tightly bound ion, inhibiting flux.
source: Modification of ring electrostatics by the polarizable hydroxyl may lead to a more tightly bound ion, inhibiting flux.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the inactivity of F80Y.

claim: If sidechain movement is required during transport, the additional hydroxyl in Tyr may introduce steric clash or competing polar interactions in alternate conformers.
source: If any sidechain movement is required during transport, the additional hydroxyl may introduce either steric clash or competing polar interactions in those alternate conformers.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the inactivity of F80Y.

claim: In F80Y, favorable hydroxide-phenyl interactions with the neighboring F83 could inhibit sidechain movement.
source: In the case of F80Y, favorable hydroxide-phenyl interactions with the neighboring F83 could also inhibit sidechain movement.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the inactivity of F80Y.

claim: The full activity of F80M may be rationalized by the F--coordinating γ-methylene, whose weakly electropositive character recalls the electropositive, edge-on presentation of the Phe ring to its coordinated F- ion.
source: Also surprising is the full activity of the F80M substitution. This may be rationalized by the F--coordinating γ-methylene, whose weakly electropositive character recalls the electropositive, edge-on presentation of the Phe ring to its coordinated F- ion.
evidence: This is an inference combining structural observations with electrostatic reasoning.

claim: The Met side-chain configuration in the F80M structure is in striking agreement with the idea that the γ-methylene mimics the Phe ring.
source: The Met side-chain configuration in the F80M structure is in striking agreement with this idea, but the functional impairment of F83M, which offers a similar configuration, remains puzzling.
evidence: This is an observation from the F80M crystal structure.

claim: The functional impairment of F83M remains puzzling despite its similar configuration to F80M.
source: The Met side-chain configuration in the F80M structure is in striking agreement with this idea, but the functional impairment of F83M, which offers a similar configuration, remains puzzling.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of F80M and F83M data.

claim: F83 coordinates its fluoride in conjunction with H106, which is the only other residue that will brook no substitution.
source: F83 coordinates its fluoride in conjunction with H106, which is the only other residue in this construct that will brook no substitution.
evidence: This combines structural observations with mutagenesis data.

claim: More precise orientation may be required at F83 than at F80.
source: This raises the possibility that more precise orientation is required here than at F80.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the differential behavior of F80M and F83M.

claim: M. tuberculosis Fluc replaces both the histidine and phenylalanine at one position with alternate residues.
source: While the Ec2 homologue studied here is inflexible at this location, different coordination schemes are clearly possible; M. tuberculosis (Figure 1d) replaces both the histidine and phenylalanine.
evidence: This is an observation from sequence alignments shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Aliphatic mutations at the critical Phe positions eliminate transport.
source: Other aliphatic mutations at these critical Phe positions are known to eliminate transport (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Table 1), and this prohibition now extends to dipolar H-bond donors, with neither Ser, Thr, His, nor Gln supporting channel activity.
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Table 1.

claim: Removal of the central phenylalanines (F80I, F83I) led to a loss of fluoride density in crystal structures.
source: Previous removal of the central phenylalanines (F80I, F83I) led to a loss of fluoride density in crystal structures (Last et al., 2016), suggesting that the F83M and F80Y mutants inhibit transport via a mechanism fundamentally different from the simple loss of a binding site.
evidence: This is a reference to prior structural data.

claim: The F83M and F80Y mutants inhibit transport via a mechanism fundamentally different from the simple loss of a binding site.
source: Previous removal of the central phenylalanines (F80I, F83I) led to a loss of fluoride density in crystal structures (Last et al., 2016), suggesting that the F83M and F80Y mutants inhibit transport via a mechanism fundamentally different from the simple loss of a binding site.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing different mutant structures.

claim: The center of the pore has an exceptionally strict requirement for F- coordination and transport.
source: The results establish that the center of the pore has an exceptionally strict requirement for F- coordination and transport, possibly reflecting a need for a geometrically precise, electrostatically weak binding partner for rapid transit of F- in this anhydrous region.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mutagenesis data.

claim: The strict requirement at the pore center possibly reflects a need for a geometrically precise, electrostatically weak binding partner for rapid transit of F- in this anhydrous region.
source: The results establish that the center of the pore has an exceptionally strict requirement for F- coordination and transport, possibly reflecting a need for a geometrically precise, electrostatically weak binding partner for rapid transit of F- in this anhydrous region.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the strict requirements at the pore center.

claim: Along the conserved polar track, only two H-bond donors are required: N41 and H106.
source: Along the conserved polar track, only two H-bond donors are required: N41 and H106.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mutagenesis data.

claim: N41 is among the most strictly conserved residues in the Fluc family.
source: The N41 residue, among the most strictly conserved in the Fluc family, is oriented between the two F--coordinating Phe, well positioned to hand off the anion between them.
evidence: This is an observation from sequence alignments.

claim: N41 is oriented between the two F--coordinating Phe, well positioned to hand off the anion between them.
source: The N41 residue, among the most strictly conserved in the Fluc family, is oriented between the two F--coordinating Phe, well positioned to hand off the anion between them.
evidence: This is an observation from crystal structures.

claim: H106 could catalyze dehydration as the F- ion leaves bulk water in the vestibule.
source: In coordinating a partially hydrated F- at the end of the pore, H106 could catalyze dehydration as the ion leaves bulk water in the vestibule.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about H106's function based on its structural position.

claim: For the hydroxyl-bearing track residues S84, S102, S110, and T114, polarity and H-bonding are not directly involved in anion permeation.
source: It is surprising, even alarming, that for the hydroxyl-bearing track residues - S84, S102, S110, and T114 - polarity and H-bonding are not directly involved in anion permeation, despite the conservation of polarity at these positions and their proximity to bound F- ions in the pore.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mutagenesis data showing that alanine substitutions retain activity.

claim: The apparent discrepancy between structural and functional facts regarding polar track residues presents a mechanistic puzzle.
source: This apparent discrepancy between structural and functional facts presents a mechanistic puzzle calling out for future attack.
evidence: This is a summary statement reflecting the current state of understanding.

claim: The 'wildtype' Ec2 construct carries a C-terminal hexahistidine tag and a single mutation (R25K) that enhances protein expression but does not affect function.
source: The 'wildtype' (WT) Ec2 construct used here carries a C-terminal hexahistidine tag as well as a single mutation (R25K) that enhances protein expression but does not affect function (Stockbridge et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental construct with a citation to prior work.

claim: Most mutants express to levels comparable to WT.
source: Most mutants express to levels comparable to WT, and all run as monodisperse homodimers on gel filtration.
evidence: This is an observation from protein purification experiments.

claim: All mutants run as monodisperse homodimers on gel filtration.
source: Most mutants express to levels comparable to WT, and all run as monodisperse homodimers on gel filtration.
evidence: This is an observation from protein purification experiments.

claim: The flux assay's dynamic range is limited by the electrode time response (~1 s), equivalent to single-channel turnover rates below ~30,000 ions/sec.
source: The flux assay's dynamic range is limited by the electrode time response (~1 s), equivalent to single-channel turnover rates below ~30,000 ions/sec, roughly 4% of the WT single-channel current under similar conditions (Turman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method's limitations with a citation.

claim: The flux assay detection limit is roughly 4% of the WT single-channel current.
source: The flux assay's dynamic range is limited by the electrode time response (~1 s), equivalent to single-channel turnover rates below ~30,000 ions/sec, roughly 4% of the WT single-channel current under similar conditions (Turman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the electrode response time and WT flux rate.
